reason: The Book of Ruth subverts rather than supports the claim that the elite are inherently better. Ruth, a poor foreign woman of low social status, is portrayed as extraordinarily virtuous (described as a "woman of valor" - אֵשֶׁת חַיִל). She is elevated through character and covenant loyalty rather than social standing. Boaz, though wealthy and of high standing, is praised not for inherent superiority due to his elite status, but for his hesed (loving-kindness) and justice in helping the vulnerable. The narrative culminates in Ruth—a non-Israelite outsider—becoming part of the royal lineage of King David, suggesting divine favor rests on virtue and faith, not elite birth. The text consistently presents moral worth as independent of, and sometimes inversely related to, wealth and social position.
